title: first
html:
Welcome to my first serious post. I'll try to keep it like a brief stroll. 

After ~3 months of reading LessWrong, consuming the median AI Twitter feed, working on a couple projects, I want to talk about (in decreasing order of importance for this post):

  1. The past: Where am I coming from? What have I witnessed?
  2. The present: What am I living through? What cost does it have?
  3. The future: Where does it go from here? Can I shape it in any way? 

[images by chatgpt. text mine]

The past

I haven't just stumbled into the AI Safety sphere. It's a forced choice. The AI Safety sphere is the least likely place for me to be in. And now, I want to be here. Here, I'm taking a look back to answer why. 

I started my bachelor's in electrical engineering in 2021. Covid times. I had no clue what I wanted to do in the future. The future was just something I'd deal with later. I was also 19, so I won't beat myself up too much over this. In late 2022, I think, I just glanced at the laptop of the person sitting in front of me in a class. I saw text stream on the screen, as if someone was texting them. But I could tell they weren't texting anyone. What the hell is that? A huge part of me wishes that I should've gotten to the bottom of it right then. I didn't. I finally came closer about six months later. Our university had an amazing research center. One of the best in my state, I'd wager. That summer, I got to work on pre-training a large language model in Marathi. I don't think I appreciated the chance enough. But I read words like pre-training, post-training, and whatnot. Lots of LangChain. OpenAI gave $10 worth of API credits for free if you signed up for ChatGPT back then. I never saw the promise of it. The models just sucked so bad. We were trying to get a model to accurately answer questions about train schedules with just a csv file containing train routes. It was a nightmare. We just couldn't get it to work. You see, we didn't even have coding agents back then. All the code had to come after looking up the LangChain docs. What a weird world. 

I simply didn't see the point of it. I could tell that OpenAI wasn't going to stop training new models. Maybe I didn't have the drive to dig deeper. I had a hundred other problems to worry about instead of checking what OpenAI was up to. In my head, the world was probably going to stay the same until I graduated with my master's. I didn't anticipate that the world was going to change with the years of my early adulthood. Not even slightly. 

I flew to the US to begin my master's degree. Was it an extremely intentional move? I don't know. Many of the people I knew said it was a really good experience. "Oh yeah, this guy? He works at XYZ now, he went to the US in 2021." Oh, that sounds super impressive. I wager I'd be able to pull off some version of this if that guy did? 

2021 is the same as 2024 in my head, when I finally was getting on the plane. A really shallow sense of the passage of time, and with it, of the progress of technology that I had just witnessed firsthand. 

"Oh, is that thing that streams text on screen going to change anything? Is it going to change the world? Should I factor this in when making any important life-changing decisions?" Nope. 

This is what I had in mind. I think I still do, deep down. This world-model allowed me to take up a job (didn't matter where, what company, etc.). It allowed me to take that trip, go home to see family and friends every winter, be mad about politics on some days, and be overall ok through the years, and almost always in a better place than I was the year before. 

This model treated the world as static. Nothing ever happens. Nothing will ever change. There'll be a few bumps here and there, yeah. Come on, I'm not dumb and naive! We'll have some bad years. A few bad harvests at most. Don't worry, it'll all turn out just fine.  

Fall 2024. Now that I've started my master's and I get to make my own financial decisions, let me see what that text-streaming ChatGPT thing was really about. Might as well get their $20 subscription. It can't even help me do any coursework. Are people seriously paying for this? Plus I can't even use it enough? Like, it literally allows only 30 queries for their best model in a whole week? What? It's really not that good anyway.

Summer 2025. Oh hey, it's been almost 8 months now since I started my master's. I should probably try finding an internship for the summer. Oh no, I didn't get one. Ugh, that's ok. I really thought I would. I'm lifeguarding at the university pool instead! It's fun. Wait, this ChatGPT thing has actually gotten better, I think. Cursor is giving away free credits for a whole year?! Sign me up. They have the best selection of models out there. Hmmmm, this is serious stuff. It still can't help me create a good website, though. So much friction, prompting, re-prompting, and cursing, even. 

What if you fed this whole thing the other way around? What might happen? If you trained with ".end The ...time a upon once" instead of "Once upon a time.... The end." wouldn't that break the whole thing or something? Oh wait, so it's statistical. Ah, I see, they're just statistical machines. Makes sense. Then, I think, they're reversal invariant. Why has no one said this out loud? I think I should. Let me just push this out there. Seems like a fun thing to do. I don't have anything better to do this summer anyway. 

Oh a professor sent me their paper. They just answered the exact question I've been asking? I clearly should've cited them. Turns out LLMs are not reversal invariant? Whaaaaat? How is this possible? 

[Reads the discussion section: sees words like "thermodynamics," "signs of life."] UM hello? I think I just stepped into something that at least sounds amazing. Can we just get to the bottom of this? 

[Tries experimenting with it for almost 8 months with nothing to talk about at the end. Turns out, I didn't read enough to appreciate any nuance. No theory of change. I, just, didn't read -- a recurring theme of the past]

But hey, this master's degree is going pretty well. I took good classes and I've been learning about this LLM thing and ML in general. I can at least talk about the transformer now. Attention? It's all you need. Not sure how to code this up yet, though. 

Spring 2026. Large language models -- these really do seem to be the next big thing, huh? Will knowing about this stuff help me get a job? Oh hell yeah. The LLMs have gotten really good now. They're trying to make them more agentic I hear. I'm sure these will turn out to be really revolutionary tools. Wow, I'm clearly working on the right kind of stuff. Did I just make it? 

But why am I not landing a job yet? Probably because I don't have any work experience. Makes sense. Oh that interview didn't come through. I ended up learning a lot, though. That's ok. 

I'm actually not hearing back from most of the jobs I apply to. Most is an understatement. Well, I think the job market is just bad. Some people in my program did end up at good places, I hear. Good for them. I will too! 

But this doesn't make sense. The models have been getting really good. The o1-preview that couldn't even help me with a class in 2024 is now GPT5.x, and can now do a big part of a course project. Surely this is not nothing? Am I hearing back from fewer places because of this? Good thing I started working on LLMs anyway. But what did I actually work on? Can I talk to a random person on the ML street about it? I don't think so. I'm doomed, aren't I? 

The Present

Summer 2026. Everything seems to be going around LLMs. I took a class called Data Visualization in 2024, where our instructor showed us how different libraries existed and how they help us build amazing visualizations. It's the stuff that's supposed to speak directly to your audience. Are people interested in data visualization, data analytics and stuff like that anymore? In reality, I found myself graduating with software that did all that by just instructing it in English. As Karpathy once famously said: "The hottest new programming language is English." Everyone on AI Twitter started openly saying that they haven't written a single line of code in about 4 months. It's the beginning of the end of knowledge work as we know it, surely? 

I've come to think that knowledge work is a means to an end for all companies. It's work. It's labor. There's just really good demand for profit-making, stable and low-latency systems. So it makes sense to pay people to keep making them better -- both sides are happy. But I saw that, at least for my potential pay grade, you don't need to keep paying a human anymore. They'll  probably make mistakes, need mentorship, and require a lot of iteration. The appetite to invest in new-grads (who are also not the top-performers, perhaps) has definitely reduced -- it's my guesstimate that people will be screaming about this in about 6 months from now. (Did we stop investing in our young people, etc. It's definitely coming.)

What I hear today is every person with my background is trying to do projects using AI. Use RAG, they say. Try to reduce hallucinations, they say. Try to build better harnesses, they say. Ok yeah I'll do all that. But look, there's a very short window when this is going to matter. In fact, RAG isn't even needed today. We've got really agentic models. They look things up in the internal docs. They have an increasingly infinite context window, are getting cheaper, and make fewer mistakes. So the projects you're asking me to do today are your best guess about the present. You will keep telling me about a new thing that I need to do every month. But you'll never ask me to look up and see where we're headed with all this. I cannot be asking myself to optimize for what the technology looks like today all over again. The paradigm is becoming an ever-evolving juggernaut inching closer to words like ASI/AGI/RSI. And as I keep realizing this, sirens go off in my head. 

I see a familiar shape in all this. What'll happen to the world while I do my RAG projects? Build my harnesses? It scares me. The present comes with so much resistance and self-doubt. I'll be doing something I have been conditioned not to do. The world changed between 2024 and 2026 right before my eyes. Then, I had the time to keep up with everything that changed, thanks to my school. I could actually take classes that were directly relevant to the technology at least. 

"The world of 2026 will stay more or less the same for me, now that I know what LLMs are, what RAG is, and what agents are. Come on, it can't change too much any more." 

The past has been about realizing that this amazing new technology exists, it's here, and it's getting better. So I arrive here, in the present. It's now about realizing the mistake of assuming that the current world will stay the same. It has proven that it won't. 

Everything I wrote before this was with the benefit of hindsight, mixed with regret, and a degree of satisfaction that I realized my mistakes. But what about now? I find myself in a world that I can see is going to go along wildly different trajectories. 

I can't get even my peers to believe that the text-streaming ChatGPT thing is going to shape our lives very directly. They say it's a tough job market. The economy is bad right now. It'll bounce back up again. And then I wonder, yeah, probably. Maybe I think about the world much more differently because I'm in a weird place right now. 

But do I, really? Why do we assume that the world is static and will stay largely static? Isn't this a recurring problem? 

"Oh you're lagging behind right now because you probably don't know about building really good RL environments. Learn this and watch your career grow. It's the real bottleneck bro." 

"Just correct this one thing that's actually missing for you, and the world will finally be static for you again. Then you can go back to living your life." And I swear, I can see people telling me the same thing again and again and again every damn year. 

As I start writing about the present, I find myself full of questions. I don't seem to have as much conviction about things as I pretend to have. I'm marred by doubt about almost everything. I think it's a better place to be in than assuming otherwise. It's better than saying: "Oh I think I just need to learn to do X and then it's back to..." 

I remember seeing a Neel Nanda episode on the 80,000 hours podcast, and also on the GDM podcast hosted by Hannah Fry. Really smart dude, I thought. Let me just follow him on LinkedIn. One day, he posts: "You should try BlueDot's courses if you're interested in AI Safety." 

That was April, 2026. Just before my graduation. I said, sure, sign me up. Back then, I was taking a class on LLMs at my school during my last semester. And our professor had given us so much stuff to read throughout the class. I was invested in this. And safety sounded like a step further from LLMs. 

I got rejected. Couldn't get in. What the hell, I thought. It was a free, introductory course, to just know about what AI Safety is about. I persisted. I took part in their first mechanistic interpretability puzzle, got a correct solution.

I applied again in June, and I got in. From July 1st to July 5th, I tried going over all the material in their course. It was so much to take in. Looking back, I realize I couldn't have covered all that material in 5 days. But I tried and took part in the discussions. For the first time ever, I thought, we should probably take a step back and slow down developing AI. I didn't have a particularly nuanced view of this, but after going through all those papers in 5 days my brain yelled "clearly no one understands where this is going and we're handing it more stuff to do?" 

I actually had zero depth back then. I was just getting started as of July 1st. Funnily enough, in my head, it was something like "oh you know, just learn about AI Safety, and then..." 

Back in Fall 2025, when I was struggling with a small transformer learning some synthetic data, I knew I was doing some work, but it totally lacked a theory of change. What happens if grokking exists in memorization? What do you want to do with it other than observing and noting it? Safety gave my obsession a channel. I was obsessed with LLMs and was actively trying to learn more about them way before I tried to learn about AI safety. I don't think it was a wrong starting point. The point is that I took safety to heart. 

I felt like I was reading something that had the potential to change a lot of my world. I'd never had a realization like this before in my life. And looking back, I realize these realizations are extremely rare and you should absolutely keep chasing these. 

I was far from "if anyone builds it everyone dies." I actually abandoned reading much of safety relevant literature after BlueDot. But I just kept picking it back up again, over and over. I found that it left me asking more questions. The obsession from the reversal-invariance days never really left me.

There was also a huge component of "You know, this is the frontier. Being here means that you'll be amongst a select few people." I can't ignore this either. I think about safety because somewhere I think very few people do. If I'd had an inkling that there were many people working on this already, I probably wouldn't have had the motivation to carry on. 

Work around alignment satisfies my intellectual curiosity and also gives me a handle that can shape the world.

So here I stand. 

The future

Alignment, for me personally, risks becoming another thing I have to do before the world becomes static. But I'd argue I'm way past that point. I've absorbed the transience of the present to the point where I freeze thinking about all of it. I feel powerless in the face of what's coming. Instead of trying to preserve the image of a static world, I find myself accepting whatever seems to be coming my way. I wait for OpenAI to release their next big model, for Anthropic to announce that they've hit RSI, for an AI model to perform Nobel prize-worthy science, or for governments to announce a pause in development. 

I hate this helpless and powerless wait. It feels like I've been robbed of any agency. 

But wasn't this feeling the same before too? I don't think the past world offered me control over my future either. In fact, I had a flawed model of the future back then. I had already been saying "do this one more thing before you go back happily to your world." 

Now that I come to terms with how the world is going to change, I should feel more engaged, invested, and I should go all in. But I just don't feel that. I think this is a skill issue and I will solve this on my own time off the blog. 

Overall, I know that my current world model is much more coherent and practical than my previous one, and if anything, I am opening myself up to more agency and not less. This space is nascent. I know for a fact that we're in the beginning of the alignment story. 

At this point, I don't think I have much more to say about the future, so I'd wind this down rather than saying hollow words that I don't really believe in.

I've found enough evidence to call this an inflection point in my life and for the world. The world will either go through a successful intelligence explosion and we'll all live to see the benefits of it, or we'll go through a period of loss of control, disruption and general instability. A lot of people think the latter is currently just as likely as the former, and that's reason enough to put my time and energy into it. 

How exactly? I will try to figure this out fast. My north star is captured really well by what Stephen Casper once said in a talk:

If you're not clear on whether and how your project might change the world (or change you), maybe try a different one. (also be a maverick)

-Mihir
